strengths: Novel and practically motivated problem formulation: the paper is, to the authors' knowledge, the first to address distractor handling in the cross-scene generalizable 3DGS setting, which is a genuine gap since existing distractor-free methods (RobustNeRF, NeRF-HuGS, On-the-go, SLS) are all scene-specific.

Well-motivated technical design: the core insight that re-rendered reference non-distractor regions from the inferred 3DGS are reliable and can be used to filter misclassified regions in the query-view robust mask is intuitive and grounded in multi-view consistency; the decoupling of disparity-induced error masks (Eq. 7) is a clean, deterministic solution to a real confound.

Comprehensive evaluation protocol covering three regimes (re-training, pre-trained models, fine-tuning) on real data (RobustNeRF, On-the-go) plus synthetic distractor data built from Re10K/ACID; the paper reports sizable gains (e.g., PSNR 21.02 vs. 15.45 baseline, 21.02 vs. 19.29 for the best transferred masking method) and shows the generalizable mask prediction outperforms scene-specific methods without mask supervision.

Thorough ablations that isolate each component (reference-based mask prediction, mask refinement, aux loss, reference scoring, distractor pruning), plus sensitivity analysis of K, N, and ρRef, and an honest limitations section (common occlusions, efficiency cost).
Efficiency analysis is included (Tab. 5), and code/models are promised to be released.
weaknesses: Evaluation scale is limited: quantitative results are averaged over roughly five test scenes from two small mobile-captured datasets, and training uses only On-the-go outdoor scenes. The cross-scene generalization claim (outdoor→indoor) rests on a very small number of scenes; more scenes or larger-scale datasets would substantially strengthen the claims.

Fairness of comparisons is questionable in places: DGGS's two-stage inference accesses an enlarged scene-images pool (K=8 vs. N=4 references) at test time, so part of the gain over DGGS-TR and baselines may come from simply having more candidate views rather than better distractor handling; although Tab. 4 attempts to control for this, the protocol (pool construction relative to the query) is nonstandard and could advantage the proposed method.

Strong dependence on external priors: the pipeline relies on a pre-trained Entity Segmentation model for mask filling/refinement, and the foundational robust-mask heuristic with fixed hyperparameters ρ1, ρ2 inherited from RobustNeRF. The framework's claim of being 'seamlessly integrated' with arbitrary generalizable 3DGS backbones is demonstrated only with Mvsplat; results with at least one other backbone (e.g., pixelsplat) would be needed to support generality.

The baseline augmentation strategy (transferring scene-specific mask prediction methods into the query rendering loss) may under-represent the true potential of competing approaches; e.g., NeRF-HuGS and SLS were designed around per-scene optimization machinery that does not transfer trivially, so the comparison against these adapted baselines may overstate the margin.

Pipeline complexity: the method stacks many components (robust mask, reference filtering, warping, decoupling, entity segmentation fill, aux loss, two-stage scoring, pruning), each with thresholds and design choices, making reproducibility and analysis of failure modes harder; the pruning strategy itself admits white speckle artifacts under common occlusions.
Several important details (synthetic data construction, training details, additional results) are deferred to an appendix not provided, so some claims cannot be fully verified from the main paper.

strengths: Addresses a relevant and practically motivated problem (distractors in generalizable, feedforward 3DGS), and the claim of being the first to explore 'Distractor-free Generalizable 3DGS' as a task appears credible.

The proposed pipeline is reasonably complete: a reference-based mask prediction plus refinement module for training robustness, and a two-stage inference framework (reference scoring + 3D distractor pruning) that addresses artifacts at test time.

Quantitative improvements are substantial on the presented benchmarks (e.g., 21.02 vs. 15.45 PSNR over the masked baseline, 21.74 with the inference framework), and ablations (Tables 2 and 4, Figures 8 and 9) cover most of the proposed components, including K/N sensitivity and pruning.
The paper is honest about limitations (common occlusions, efficiency cost), and the fine-tuning experiments (Table 3) provide an additional evaluation angle.
weaknesses: Novelty is largely compositional: the core mask heuristic comes from RobustNeRF, masking/segmentation from Entity Segmentation/SAM-style models, the backbone from Mvsplat, and pruning is a straightforward removal of decoded attributes. The individual technical contributions are incremental and the paper reads more as careful system engineering than a new method.

Heavy reliance on a pre-trained segmentation model weakens the headline claim of 'generalizable mask prediction without any mask supervision' that outperforms scene-specific methods; a significant portion of mask quality likely derives from the external segmentation prior. A dedicated, quantitative mask-accuracy evaluation (e.g., IoU against ground-truth masks, and an ablation swapping in other segmentation models) is needed to support this claim.

Evaluation scale is small: only about five test scenes (RobustNeRF + two On-the-go scenes), with a single backbone (Mvsplat). The cross-scene generalization claim (outdoor training, indoor inference) rests on very limited data, and no results with a second backbone (e.g., pixelsplat) are reported despite it being listed as a baseline.

The evaluation protocol is convoluted and partially favorable to the method: the scene-images pool at test time is constructed with views closest to the query and curated to include distractor-free images, which is precisely the information the Reference Scoring mechanism needs; although the authors acknowledge this is 'only for validation', the main quantitative tables still depend on this setup.

Several claims lack direct evidence: the assertion that distractors 'severely impair' learning of 3D consistency is supported mainly by qualitative figures; failure cases of the mask refinement (e.g., when entity segmentation fails on unusual distractors) are not analyzed; and the appendix, which contains key dataset-construction and training details, is not part of the submission provided for review.

Presentation is dense and error-prone (e.g., inconsistent notation for masks across Secs. 4.1-4.2, grammatical issues, cramped multi-panel figures), which impedes reproducibility; hyperparameter choices such as ρ1, ρ2 are deferred to prior work without discussion of sensitivity in the generalizable setting.

strengths: Introduces a new and practically relevant problem — distractor-robust *generalizable* (feedforward) 3DGS — which is a genuine gap: existing distractor-free methods (RobustNeRF, NeRF-HuGS, SpotLessSplats) are scene-specific and rely on per-scene optimization that does not transfer to cross-scene generalizable training.

The proposed training paradigm is well-motivated: using re-rendered reference views of the inferred 3DGS as a consistency-based filter for the loss-derived robust mask is an elegant way to counter the unreliability of residual-loss outliers in cross-scene training, and the mask evolution in Fig. 3 convincingly illustrates the failure modes being addressed.

Comprehensive ablations (Tab. 2, 4, Fig. 9) that decompose each component's contribution — the jump from +Robust Mask (17.11) to +Ref-based Mask Prediction (20.35) is substantial and supports the central claim.

Careful experimental protocol: compares against re-trained generalizable baselines augmented with existing masking strategies, pre-trained models, and fine-tuned variants; also constructs synthetic distractor data (COCO inserted into Re10K/ACID) for controlled verification.

The two-stage inference framework (reference scoring + 3D distractor pruning) is a reasonable and well-analyzed solution to the distinct problem of distractor artifacts at feedforward inference time, with an honest limitation discussion (common occlusions, efficiency cost).
weaknesses: Limited scale of the evidence base: all real-data training uses only a handful of On-the-go outdoor scenes and evaluation covers roughly five unseen scenes. Given that the paper's core claim is cross-scene generalization, training on so few scenes and testing on so few scenes weakens the generality claims; the synthetic experiments only support robustness to inserted distractors in a single data domain.

The framework is heavily engineered and stacks multiple off-the-shelf components (entity segmentation model, warping with predicted depth, heuristic thresholds ρ1, ρ2, ρRef). Sensitivity to the pre-trained segmentation model's quality is not analyzed — failures on atypical distractors or segmentation errors could propagate, and there is no stress test of this dependency.

The gain over the strongest existing masking baseline transferred to the generalizable setting is modest in some metrics: DGGS-TR 21.02/0.738/0.242 vs. +SLS 19.29/0.709/0.286. The PSNR improvement is clear, but SSIM/LPIPS gains are smaller, and per-scene variance/statistical significance is not reported.

Only Mvsplat is used as the backbone despite the claim that the paradigm 'can be seamlessly integrated with existing generalizable 3DGS frameworks'; demonstrating it on at least one additional backbone (e.g., pixelsplat) would substantially strengthen the contribution.

Inference requires a scene-images pool (K≥N additional views) and a two-stage forward pass, adding assumptions and cost (Tab. 5 shows ~1.8x slower than Mvsplat); the practical setting where such a pool is available deserves more scrutiny, and the reference-scoring evaluation setting (pool constructed around the query view) is somewhat favorable.

Presentation is dense and notation-heavy (multiple mask types MRob, MQ, MD, MRef, MEnRef, M), making the method harder to follow; several design details (e.g., entity-fill threshold logic, pruning conditions) are deferred and could benefit from cleaner formalization.

Claim of mask accuracy 'superior to scene-specific training methods' is based on qualitative comparison (Fig. 6) plus reconstruction metrics rather than mask-level quantitative evaluation (e.g., IoU against held-out masks), so this claim is under-supported.

strengths: Identifies and formalizes a new, practically relevant task — distractor-free generalizable 3DGS — that combines two previously separate research threads (generalizable 3DGS and scene-specific distractor-free reconstruction), and the claim of being the first to address this setting is plausible given the related work coverage.

The core insight is intuitive and well-motivated: re-rendered reference views from a feed-forward model are more stable than query renders, so non-distractor reference regions can serve as a multi-view-consistency filter to clean the initial robust masks. This is validated empirically (Table 6 shows re-render PSNR consistently exceeds query PSNR throughout training).

Comprehensive experimental design: evaluation on both real benchmarks (On-the-go, RobustNeRF) and a newly constructed synthetic distractor dataset built on Re10K/ACID; three comparison regimes (retraining, pre-trained models, fine-tuning); and a thorough set of ablations covering the mask prediction, mask refinement, segmentation model choice, mask fusion strategy, K/N reference-pool sizes, and each inference component (Tables 2, 5, 9, 11, 13).

Strong and consistent quantitative gains: 21.74 vs 15.45 PSNR over the baseline Mvsplat and 21.74 vs 19.29 over the best adapted distractor-free masking strategy under identical training conditions; feed-forward mask prediction reportedly rivals scene-specific methods (Fig. 6, B.7), which is a notable result given no mask supervision.

Fair-baseline effort is visible: the authors retrain several scene-specific distractor-free methods (RobustNeRF, On-the-go, NeRF-HuGS, SLS, HybridGS) inside the generalizable pipeline and document integration details in Appendix A.2.2, including where components (e.g., Nerfacto) had to be dropped and why.
Honest limitation discussion (common occlusions causing speckles, efficiency cost, no generative completion) and failure-case analysis (Fig. 16).
weaknesses: Novelty is primarily at the system/integration level: individual components (residual-threshold robust masks from RobustNeRF, entity segmentation for mask filling, depth-based warping, uncertainty-weighted losses from On-the-go, reference selection/pruning heuristics) are largely drawn from prior scene-specific works, and the contribution is their careful combination and adaptation to the feed-forward setting rather than a fundamentally new technique.

Evaluation scale is modest: the main Table 1 headline is a mean over five test scenes at low resolution (192x256), and per-scene numbers for the full test set are only partially reported (Statue, Android in Tab. 1; two On-the-go scenes in Tab. 12). Given the small scene count, the ~5-6 dB improvement claims would benefit from more scenes or statistical treatment.

Fairness of retrained baselines is questionable in places: NeRF-HuGS is stripped of its Nerfacto component, and scene-specific residual/uncertainty methods are transplanted into a feed-forward loss where they were never designed to operate; some reported gaps may partially reflect this mismatch rather than the proposed masking paradigm itself.

Dependence on a pretrained entity segmentation model and a hand-crafted disparity-error decoupling introduces multiple hand-tuned heuristics (thresholds ρ1, ρ2, ρRef, entity-filling rules, pruning occlusion conditions), and the paper's own ablations show the segmentation model contributes little (Tab. 5), raising the question of how much of the pipeline is actually necessary; the cumulative complexity may hurt generalization to more diverse capture conditions.

Table 7 shows DGGS-TR in a fully scene-specific setting (21.57) underperforms SLS (22.69) without distractor-free references; the striking 30.50 result requires access to distractor-free references at inference, which weakens the claim of superiority over scene-specific distractor-free methods in their native regime.

Two-stage inference roughly doubles inference cost (Table 4) and requires a scene-images pool (K >= N views), which changes the deployment assumptions relative to standard 2-image feed-forward baselines; the comparison of efficiency and settings against Pixelsplat/Mvsplat is therefore not fully like-for-like.

Writing quality issues throughout (e.g., 'pridiction', 'candidator', 'Reprodicibility', inconsistent naming ArcdeTriomphe/Arcdetriomphe, some garbled figure annotations) and code is only promised, not released, which limits reproducibility at review time.

strengths: Identifies and formalizes a relevant, previously unexplored problem: distractor-robust training and inference for generalizable (feed-forward) 3DGS, rather than only scene-specific distractor removal.

The core observation that re-rendered reference views are more stable than query views and can be used to filter heuristic robust masks is intuitive and empirically supported (Tab. 6 shows reference re-rendering consistently outperforms query rendering throughout training).

Large quantitative gains over the baseline and over transferred scene-specific masking strategies under identical training conditions (e.g., 21.02 vs 15.45 PSNR vs Mvsplat baseline; 21.02 vs 19.29 vs the best transferred masker in Tab. 1), with reasonable component-wise ablations (Tab. 2, 5, 9, 11, 13).

Broad comparison design: retraining baselines with multiple existing distractor-free mask predictors, comparisons against pre-trained generalizable models, fine-tuning studies, and a synthetic distractor dataset built on Re10K/ACID with controlled distractor statistics.
The method is framed as a plug-in paradigm compatible with existing generalizable 3DGS backbones, which increases potential impact; authors commit to releasing code.
weaknesses: Heavy, largely heuristic pipeline: the method stacks many hand-crafted components (heuristic robust mask Eq. 4, reference re-render filter, entity-segmentation filling, disparity decoupling, auxiliary loss, two-stage inference, distractor pruning). Each piece is a known technique, and the overall contribution feels more like engineering integration than a principled new framework; sensitivity to hyperparameters (rho_1, rho_2 fixed from RobustNeRF) is under-justified for in-the-wild generalization.

Evaluation scale is small: quantitative results rest on only ~6 real test scenes (two On-the-go scenes plus four RobustNeRF scenes) at a reduced resolution of 192x256. For a paper whose central claim is generalization, this is a narrow evaluation basis, and absolute PSNR values (~21 dB) and the low resolution weaken the significance of the reported gains.

The headline claim that feed-forward mask prediction is 'superior to scene-specific distractor-free methods' is supported only by qualitative figures (Fig. 6, 12); no quantitative mask accuracy (e.g., IoU against GT masks) is reported, which is a notable gap given the abstract emphasizes this claim.

Potential circularity concerns: the reference-based filter depends on the quality of the currently trained model's re-renders, and early-training masks (Tab. 6 shows query PSNR of only 12.13 at iteration 200) may be unreliable; the paper does not analyze robustness of the iterative masking process in early training or under severe distractor density.

Several results appear favorable but hard to interpret: e.g., Tab. 7 reports 30.50 PSNR for single-scene DGGS-TR with distractor-free references, a jump far beyond all scene-specific baselines whose evaluation protocol is not fully aligned with prior work; similarly, the auxiliary loss Eq. 7 supervises reference re-rendering, which partially explains why reference re-render numbers improve, complicating the core-insight argument.

Inference requires a scene image pool (K=8) and a two-stage procedure with pre-computed segmentation, increasing cost and deviating from the standard sparse feed-forward setting (two images) that prior generalizable 3DGS works target; the comparison to Mvsplat/Pixelsplat under different input budgets is therefore not fully apples-to-apples.

The ablations show the pretrained segmentation model contributes little (Tab. 5) and SAM2 changes results only marginally, raising questions about which components are truly essential and about the framing of the contribution.

Pruning strategy is applied conditionally in a somewhat ad-hoc manner ('only where it is not considered a common occluded region'), with speckle artifacts in common-occlusion cases acknowledged as a limitation; no generative or learned completion alternative is explored.

Writing quality is uneven: frequent grammatical errors ('candidator', 'pridiction', 'Segmantation', 'It, captured using...'), and several figure/table references are imprecise, which detracts from readability and suggests insufficient polish.

strengths: Identifies a genuinely new and practically relevant task — distractor-free generalizable 3DGS — and provides a reasonably complete solution covering both training (mask prediction/refinement for robust losses) and inference (reference scoring + distractor pruning) phases.

Strong quantitative gains over the baseline and over transferred scene-specific masking methods on real benchmarks (PSNR 21.74 vs. 15.45 baseline; 21.02 vs. 19.29 vs. best transferred masking strategy), with consistent trends in qualitative comparisons.

Extensive ablations (Table 2, 5, 11, 13; Figures 3, 8, 10) that isolate the contribution of each module, plus supporting analyses such as the query vs. re-rendered reference stability study (Table 6) that underpins the core insight of the method.

Well-scoped experimental protocol: fair re-training comparisons under identical settings on established distractor datasets (RobustNeRF, On-the-go), a controlled synthetic distractor dataset built on Re10K/ACID for verification, and fine-tuning experiments comparing against SLS-style scene-specific strategies.
Transparent about limitations (common occlusions, efficiency cost) and includes failure case analysis, which strengthens credibility.
weaknesses: Generality of the 'plug-in' claim is under-supported: the framework is only demonstrated with Mvsplat as the backbone; no results with Pixelsplat or other generalizable 3DGS architectures despite the claim of seamless integration into 'existing frameworks'.

The claim that feed-forward mask prediction 'achieves accuracy superior to scene-specific Distractor-free methods' is supported mainly by qualitative mask visualizations (Figs. 6, 12); no quantitative mask metrics (e.g., IoU/precision/recall) are reported, making the claim hard to verify.

Several transferred baselines perform worse than the unmasked baseline (e.g., +On-the-go, +HybridGS below baseline in Table 1), raising questions about whether these masking methods were optimally adapted to the feed-forward setting; only the strongest competitor (SLS) transfers reasonably.

Method is a pipeline of many heuristics (robust mask initialization, reference warping filter, mask decoupling, segmentation-based filling, scoring, pruning) with multiple hand-tuned thresholds (ρ1, ρ2, ρRef), which raises concerns about robustness and hyperparameter sensitivity in broader settings; only ρRef is ablated.

Evaluation scope is narrow: low resolution (192×256), few evaluation scenes (five-scene mean plus RobustNeRF), and synthetic distractors that are inserted with fixed consistency across views may not fully reflect real transient-object dynamics.

Efficiency cost of the two-stage inference and segmentation model is non-trivial (Table 4), and the paper has notable writing issues (e.g., 'candidator', 'pridiction') and presentation density in the method section that hamper readability.
